topic.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection and Open-World Reliability
topic.overview: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input lies outside the conditions a model was trained to handle. These papers use likelihood ratios, nearest neighbors, gradients, logits, and information decomposition to identify unfamiliar examples. A representative training approach accounts for the discrepancy between auxiliary outliers available during training and the unseen outliers encountered later.
topic.whyItMatters: A classifier can be confident on inputs for which its labels or learned relationships no longer apply. Reliable detection can support abstention or further review, but performance on one curated outlier set does not establish broad open-world reliability.
topic.evolution: The representatives develop semantic and density-based detectors before exploring feature geometry and distributional augmentation. Recent work extends detection to tabular foundation models and graphs, where changes in node attributes and connectivity introduce distinct sources of unfamiliarity.
openQuestions: How can evaluations cover shifts that differ substantially from training-time outliers?
Which detection signals remain reliable while preserving accuracy on difficult but legitimate inputs?
